name: France (Fifth Republic)
summary: France under the Fifth Republic, founded by Charles de Gaulle in 1958. After decolonisation it became a founding power of European integration.

location.value: Western Europe, from the Rhine to the Atlantic, plus overseas regions and territories.

terrain.value: Plains, the Alps, Pyrenees and Massif Central.

climate.value: Temperate in the north and west, continental in the east, Mediterranean in the south.

resources.value: Rich farmland, wine regions, forests and a large nuclear power industry (about 70% of electricity).

disasters.value: The 2003 heatwave killed about 15,000 people; floods and storms.

urbanisation.value: About 80% urban; Paris is by far the largest city, with over 12 million in its metropolitan area.

disease.value: AIDS from the 1980s; COVID-19. A universal public health system.

migration.value: Migration from North Africa and elsewhere.

tradeRoutes.value: Part of the EU single market; global trade through ports such as Le Havre and Marseille.

wealth.value: A high-income economy; one of the largest in the world.

moneyAndTax.value: The new franc (1960), then the euro (2002); high taxes pay for social services.

inequality.value: A strong welfare state keeps inequality lower than in many rich countries; tensions in poorer suburbs.

governmentType.value: A semi-presidential republic: a powerful elected president and a prime minister responsible to parliament.

keyRulers.value: Charles de Gaulle, François Mitterrand, Jacques Chirac.

succession.value: Direct presidential elections (since 1962) and parliamentary elections.

institutions.value: The 1958 constitution of the Fifth Republic, the Constitutional Council, and a centralised civil service.

stability.value: Generally stable; the May 1968 protests and strikes shook the government.

eliteConflict.value: Competition between left- and right-wing parties, and since 2017 new centrist and populist parties.

armyAndTech.value: A nuclear power with a permanent UN Security Council seat.

majorWars.value: The Algerian War ended in 1962; later military operations in Africa and the Middle East.

territoryChange.value: Algeria and most African colonies became independent around 1960–62.

alliancesRivals.value: Founding member of the European Union; a NATO member (left its command 1966–2009).

inventions.value: The TGV high-speed train, Concorde (with Britain), Ariane rockets, the Minitel.

scienceEducation.value: Free public education; elite grandes écoles; strong research in physics and mathematics.

openness.value: Leading role in European integration; open to world culture while protecting French language and film.

communicationTransport.value: The TGV high-speed train (1981), the Paris Métro, motorways and the Channel Tunnel (1994).

religion.value: A secular state (laïcité); mostly Catholic tradition; a large Muslim minority.

languageWriting.value: French, protected by law; regional languages such as Breton and Occitan.

artsArchitecture.value: New Wave cinema, fashion houses, the Pompidou Centre and the Louvre Pyramid.

socialStructure.value: A large middle class; debates about immigration and integration.

sharedIdentity.value: Republican values of “Liberty, Equality, Fraternity” and a strong national culture.

dailyLife.value: Apartments in cities, houses in the countryside; bread, cheese, wine; long family lunches.

neighbours.value: Belgium, Germany, Switzerland, Italy, Spain, UK.

ideasReligions.value: Laïcité (strict separation of religion and state) and existentialist philosophy.

riseSignals.value: Charles de Gaulle’s new constitution (1958) gave the government more stability than the Fourth Republic.

peakPeriod.value: Still exists; the “Trente Glorieuses” boom (1945–1975) was a high point of growth.

declineSignals.value: Not applicable: still exists. Debates over debt, protests and social cohesion.

outcome.value: Continues today as the French Republic.
